picked.t: Vietnamese trainees in Germany fight to move beyond ‘cheap labor’ image
picked.body: When Nguyen Van Bau arrived in Germany at 19 to begin vocational training at a hotel in Bavaria, he expected to learn the hospitality business. Instead, he found himself delivering bread for his boss and doing manual work such as clearing broken tiles from holiday apartments during the pandemic. "I felt like cheap labor," Bau says. Thu Trang, 23, had a similarly difficult start at a hospital in Leipzig. She says some colleagues gave her tasks outside her job description, refused to guide her and at times blocked her opportunities to learn. "Seeing that I was a foreigner, many colleagues dumped tasks outside the job description on me," she says. "When no one was around, they glared at me, bullied me, and blocked my learning opportunities." Bau and Trang are among more than 16,000 Vietnamese pursuing vocational training in Germany, according to the country’s 2024 Migration Report. For many, the biggest challenges go beyond tuition or living costs. Limited German, unfamiliarity with labor rights and difficulty adapting to a less hierarchical workplace culture can leave trainees vulnerable to exploitation or exclusion. Bau’s family spent €7,500 (US$8,400) on agency fees in 2019 and another €11,300 on language courses, housing and financial requirements. "My parents said it was an advance on my inheritance," he says. "With such a huge sum invested, failure meant there was no way back." Although vocational trainees are supposed to receive professional instruction, Bau says he was instead assigned manual work for less than €5 an hour, around half the minimum wage at the time, while being routinely scolded and belittled. After others warned him that he was being exploited, he began studying German labor law. With support from a hospitality workers’ union, he sued his former employer over excessive overtime during peak periods and won. In 2022, he moved to another hotel where he received structured training. A year later, he graduated with top marks, was promoted to shift supervisor and was earning three times his previous salary. "The biggest change wasn’t the salary, but my standing at work," he says. "I am no longer a passive placeholder." Trang took a different route. Before choosing an agency, she first selected her school and later joined a state-supported program costing about €4,000. She began nursing training at Leipzig University Hospital in June 2024 and was the only Vietnamese student in her class. The program proved demanding. Half of the original 30 students dropped out after the first semester. Trang says fast speech, technical vocabulary and subjects such as medical ethics forced her to work much harder than local classmates. She began carrying a notebook everywhere, writing down unfamiliar medical terms and the names of equipment she encountered. Before lessons, she searched for materials in Vietnamese and then translated them into German to prepare herself. "You can’t just blindly stumble through the medical field," she says. As her language skills improved, so did her confidence. She began refusing tasks she considered unreasonable and says she learned that speaking up often led to greater respect from colleagues. "I learned that daring to speak up earns you respect in this environment," she says. Taking control In 2024, Bau and two colleagues founded a company that recruits young Vietnamese for vocational training in Germany without charging them agency fees. Instead, the company receives €5,000 from German employers for each successful recruit. Applicants are expected to hold at least a B1 German certificate, or A2 combined with strong communication and problem-solving skills. Bau says the company places more emphasis on practical ability and how candidates respond to real situations than on qualifications alone. Language remains one of the biggest weaknesses among Vietnamese trainees. Christopher Gnadt, a lecturer at the University of Vechta with more than a decade of experience recruiting and managing nursing-home staff, says two issues often put Vietnamese workers at a disadvantage: weak German and a tendency to remain too deferential. "German employers do not expect an employee who simply knows how to obey," he says. "Timidity and reluctance to ask questions are often perceived as lack of competence." Nguyen Thi Loan, a nurse in her 30s in North Rhine-Westphalia, says her own experience shows how much language can change a migrant worker’s position. Born into a low-income family in Hanoi’s Soc Son District, she won a place in an affordable vocational training program in Germany because of her strong academic record. Today, she works as a practical instructor at four elderly-care facilities and operates a support hotline for Vietnamese trainees. She also helps her husband recruit Vietnamese workers for German employers and runs an SOS service for trainees facing problems with study, work or integration. picked.t: How Australia's tighter visa rules might affect international students' study and migration pathways
picked.body: Hong Hai, from Hai Phong, arrived in Australia last year on a 462 visa, which allows holders to work and travel. After doing some research, he learned that Tasmania offered relatively favorable policies for international students and faced worker shortages. He planned to pursue vocational training, find a job and eventually seek permanent residency. While Hai was researching how to apply for a student visa (subclass 500), the Australian government announced a series of tighter policies affecting foreigners. As announced by the Australian government, starting Oct. 2, international students will only be allowed to progress to higher levels of study, rather than repeatedly enrolling in courses at the same or a lower level, under Australia's student visa (subclass 500) rules. Most foreigners and international students in Australia can no longer apply for a student visa from within the country. According to Australia's Department of Home Affairs, students seeking this type of visa must now apply and wait for a decision from outside Australia. The department late last month also announced that Australia will stop foreign students from bringing partners and children to accompany them while they study, with certain exemptions for students from ASEAN and Pacific nations, and those taking PhD courses. After seeing the high student visa refusal rate, Hai became uncertain about whether he should apply for another Australian visa. If rejected, he would not only lose his application fee but also have the refusal recorded in his immigration history, potentially creating obstacles when applying for visas in some other countries. Australian Department of Home Affairs data show that the student visa refusal rate reached 24.2% in June 2026, meaning roughly one in four applications was refused. ABC reported that this was the highest refusal rate in a decade, up from 7.9% in June 2016. "I feel that policies are becoming increasingly difficult for immigrants, especially international students," Hai said. Over the past three years, the Australian government has taken various measures to control net migration as inflation has pushed up housing and other living costs. International students, who account for about one-third of temporary visa holders, have become a key target of these efforts. Since 2024, Australia has raised student visa fees three times, shortened the post-study work period for international graduates and increased financial proof requirements, among other measures. Shortly before announcing the latest regulations, the government last month barred a postgraduate course that was reportedly being used by some international students as a pathway to permanent residency. Genuine students face fewer roadblocks Experts say the new policies will have a greater impact on people who study primarily to extend their legal stay and pursue migration pathways than on those with genuine study goals and clear plans. "A strategy that is primarily based on securing a visa first and then finding a way to stay and migrate will become more uncertain," said Professor Ly Tran Thi of Deakin University. She said Vietnamese students, as nationals of an ASEAN country, as well as PhD students, will still be allowed to bring family members to Australia under the new rules. This provides a degree of stability for them and their families. Nguyen Duc Quyet, CEO and co-founder of education and migration consultancy Rightway, added that applicants for Master by Research programs may also be allowed to bring family members, as these programs could fall under the category of "postgraduate research programs." However, he said this needs to be confirmed by official regulations. Based on individual states' workforce attraction strategies and the government's latest direction, migration opportunities are increasingly concentrated in five groups of occupations, according to Nguyen Duy Tung, an Australian migration representative at Rightway Education & Services, a consultancy specializing in Australian study, migration and skills assessment, with offices in Melbourne, Adelaide and Ho Chi Minh City. They include construction and infrastructure; healthcare and health services; education and teaching; agriculture, fisheries and resources; and security, defense and policing, he said. Skilled visas such as subclasses 491, 190 and 494, which are commonly pursued after subclass 500 or 485 visas, remain a priority in regional areas. These areas are outside major cities such as Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. Students can receive an additional one to two years on their 485 visas in regional areas, giving them more time to gain work experience and accumulate points for migration. However, Professor Ly cautioned international students against assuming that studying a particular field will guarantee a pathway to permanent residency, as labor market demand changes over time and migration policies change accordingly. picked.t: Da Nang accommodation options cater to different travel needs
picked.body: For some visitors, a Da Nang trip starts with an early walk along My Khe Beach. Others prioritize food, sightseeing or time with family. The best accommodation therefore depends less on the number of facilities or the lowest advertised rate than on three factors: group size, length of stay and how much time guests expect to spend at the property. Location and hotels for shorter stays Travelers should first choose an area based on their itinerary before comparing accommodation. Those planning to swim or walk along the shore may prefer My Khe Beach, while visitors focused on the Museum of Cham Sculpture, city dining and walks along Bach Dang Street may find the central area more convenient. For mixed itineraries, comparing travel times to frequently visited places can help identify the most practical location. Everyday convenience, such as easy access to breakfast or a quick trip back with tired children, may matter more than proximity to a single attraction. For couples, solo travelers and small families on short visits, a beachfront hotel can make the coast part of the daily routine while providing services such as breakfast, housekeeping and reception support. A comfortable room may be sufficient for guests who spend most of their time exploring the city. Before booking, travelers should check the property's exact location and beach access, bed arrangements and included services. Apartments when daily routines matter For longer stays, a kitchen, laundry facilities and a separate workspace can be more useful than hotel services. Self-catering apartments can suit families with young children, remote workers and travelers who prefer to prepare some meals themselves. Layouts vary from studios with kitchenettes to larger units with separate bedrooms, living areas and full kitchens. Travelers should check the appliances and cooking equipment provided, laundry arrangements and cleaning schedules. For extended stays, they should also confirm whether electricity, water and other charges are included. Remote workers should verify the availability of a suitable workspace and reliable internet connection rather than relying solely on a general Wi-Fi listing. Whole-house villas for larger groups For larger families or groups of friends, an entire villa can provide shared living space while allowing guests to stay under one roof. Hanami Villa Da Nang at 276/7 Ngu Hanh Son Street is one example. According to its operator, the property is rented as a whole and has six bedrooms, shared living areas, a private pool, two kitchens, a cinema room, a steam room and a rooftop area. The operator says it can accommodate up to 16 guests. The villa is in a residential area rather than directly on the beachfront. It is managed by Nami Stay , which provides local support during guests' stays. For larger rentals, travelers should check the floor plan, bed allocation, stairs and bathroom access, particularly when traveling with people with limited mobility. Families should also ask about pool safety and other measures before arrival. Price comparisons should cover the full stay rather than the advertised nightly rate alone. Travelers should compare the same dates and group size while checking taxes, mandatory fees, deposits, cleaning or utility charges, cancellation terms and extra-person fees. For villas, they should also confirm whether the booking provides exclusive use of the property. Weather is another consideration. When rain disrupts outdoor plans, indoor communal space can become particularly useful for families and groups. Ultimately, a beachfront hotel can suit shorter stays centered on sightseeing and the coast, an apartment can support longer-term daily routines, while a whole-house villa can give larger groups more shared space. The best choice is the one whose location, layout, services and booking terms match the travelers and their plans, rather than simply the property that looks most appealing in photographs.

picked.t: Why are Korean visitors to Vietnam declining?
picked.body: Vietnam welcomed 17.7 million international visitors in the first nine months, up almost 15% year-on-year, the General Statistics Office reported. South Korea ranked second, after mainland China, with 3 million arrivals, but was the only top-10 market to record a decline, down about 5%. Korean arrivals also fell 5% in 2025, when total arrivals hit a record of more than 21 million. South Koreans made over 19 million overseas trips in the first eight months, up 2%, according to the Korea Tourism Organization. Martin Koerner, commercial director of Anam Group, which manages two resorts in Mui Ne and Cam Ranh, says Korean demand is still growing but shifting elsewhere. Yanolja Research found that only three of the 12 most-visited destinations for Koreans grew in the first half. Japan rose 18.6% to 5.6 million visits, 40% of Korean outbound travelers. Mainland China rose 16%, while Macau grew 0.7%. The other nine destinations, mostly in Southeast Asia and the U.S., all declined. Vietnam fell more than 2%, and Thailand dropped the most, at 24%. Pham Hai Quynh, director of the Asia Tourism Development Institute, attributes the decline partly to growing competition from China and Japan. Quynh says Japan offers a good exchange rate, easy transport and quality service. China has attractive tour prices, visa-free entry for Koreans since late 2025 and more direct flights. A weak won is a factor. The currency fell to 1,536 won per U.S. dollar on June 3, its lowest since 2009, and now sits around 1,350. Korea JoongAng Daily reports that the weak currency is changing how South Koreans travel. They are shopping less, opting for Airbnb-style rentals over luxury hotels. Hanatour, one of South Korea's largest travel companies, says Korean travelers used to favor cheap tours with shopping stops. Now they choose pricier packages without shopping to cut down on extra spending. However, travel spending in Japan continues to rise, as the weak yen makes the destination more affordable. In 2025, South Korean visitors spent a record $5.7 billion in Japan. Koerner adds that beyond cost, the convenience of the trip also shapes Korean choices. A flight of two to three hours to Japan or China beats a six-hour trip to Southeast Asia. "In this context, Vietnam's edge as a low-cost destination no longer creates a big enough gap to hold on to Korean visitors," Quynh says. Saturation is another problem. Quynh says a destination's life cycle lasts three to four years, after which travelers seek something new. Da Nang, Nha Trang and Phu Quoc have been promoted in Korea since around 2023, and golf and spa packages have grown familiar. Fewer flights have hurt too. Higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict led Korean airlines, mainly low-cost carriers, to cut 1,000 flights between April and June. Yanolja Research also says Vietnam's image has been linked to Cambodian scam compounds. Negative sentiment toward Vietnam once reached 18%. To win Koreans back, Quynh says Vietnam should refresh its image, rely less on cheap beach holidays, and develop cultural, ecological and wellness products. He also urges more promotion in Busan, Daegu and Gwangju cities. According to ET News , Vietnam remains the most popular Southeast Asian destination among South Koreans. Koerner says Vietnam needs to offer new experiences to bring back Korean travelers, many of whom have already visited the country. He states destinations, airlines, hotels, travel companies and online travel agencies should work together on packages with competitive prices and appealing experiences. Promotions also need to come sooner, as Korean travelers book just weeks before departure rather than months ahead. "The most important question is how Vietnam can beat its rivals and become the top choice at the moment travelers decide to book," he says.

picked.t: Residents wade through half-meter floodwaters as year's highest tide swamps Ho Chi Minh City streets
picked.body: At around 4 p.m., a tide of more than 1.7 m, the highest in HCMC this year, leaves Pham Huu Lau Street in the former District 7 in the city's southern area under half a meter of water along a stretch of about 3 km. picked.t: Hanoi kicks off $4.94B investment push across 18 key projects
picked.body: The city announced 292 projects with a combined investment of VND384.886 trillion (US$14.92 billion), including 18 key projects worth VND127.46 trillion, focusing on transport, infrastructure, environmental protection and public services. A highlight was the opening to technical traffic of a 15 km section of the Ring Road 4 parallel road, from the Huu Hong dyke-Hong Ha Bridge area to Thang Long Boulevard. The 58.2 km project, launched in June 2023, has reached about 90% completion. Hanoi plans to open two more sections totaling 22 km in November and complete the entire parallel road this year. Three sections of Ring Road 2.5, spanning 2.2 km, are also among the featured projects, alongside Yen So Bus station, designed to handle 800-1,000 vehicle trips daily, and the second facility of Hanoi Heart Hospital, which will provide 300 beds. New transport and logistics projects include an elevated road along Co Linh Street linking to the Hanoi-Hai Phong Expressway and Giang Bien inland waterway port, which is expected to strengthen freight connections with the northern port system. Environmental projects include a scheme to upgrade dykes, dredge and tackle pollution along the Nhue River, with a preliminary investment of more than VND75 trillion, and a VND11.681 trillion project to clean up the Cau Bay River. A wastewater collection and treatment system in western Hanoi is also planned. In industry, the first phase of Tien Thang Industrial Park will cover more than 230 ha, with an investment of VND4.455 trillion, and is expected to create over 16,000 jobs. Tourism and cultural developments include a cultural and commercial space along 131 railway arches near Long Bien Bridge, a 299 ha Ba Vi Safari Park outside Ba Vi National Park, and a multi-purpose entertainment complex featuring a horse-racing track in Soc Son, with investment of $420 million. A hotel, office and commercial complex in Dong Anh will receive investment of $120 million. Hanoi will also develop three modern multi-level schools in Thach That, Soc Son and Phu Dong. A cybersecurity center and centralized data center, worth nearly VND4.5 trillion, are scheduled for completion in February 2028. At the ceremony, Chairman of the municipal People’s Committee Vu Dai Thang urged investors and project owners to ensure timely implementation, maintain construction quality and avoid cost overruns. He also called for faster resolution of land clearance and infrastructure bottlenecks, while ensuring labor safety and minimizing disruption to residents.

picked.t: HCMC teen with IELTS 9.0 and top English awards for gifted students chooses teaching career
picked.body: Nguyen Tuan Phong is a former English major at Tran Dai Nghia High School for the Gifted in Ho Chi Minh City. He is currently enrolled in the university's English language teacher education program. He said he began considering a career in teaching early in 10th grade, after being selected for the national English competition team and winning second prize. The achievement motivated him but also brought considerable pressure. Phong repeatedly questioned whether he could continue improving and maintain his performance. Encouraged and inspired by the teachers who coached the competition team, he gradually regained his confidence and went on to win first prize in the competition for two consecutive years. "I also want to become a friendly teacher with strong professional knowledge who inspires students, just like the teachers I have learned from," Phong said. Phong took the IELTS test in 11th grade to strengthen his university application. Because the test came immediately after the national English competition, he did not have much time to prepare and aimed for a score of 8.0. He was therefore surprised to receive a perfect score. "I couldn't believe my eyes. I thought the sheet showing a score of 9.0 was just a sample result. Only after reading it carefully did I confirm that it was actually mine," he said. Phong said he had been exposed to English since the age of four and continued taking classes at language centers until the end of middle school. Initially, he was eager to learn English so he could watch foreign reality shows, movies, and cartoons. Over time, he shifted toward scientific content and materials related to his school curriculum. English, to him, became a "gateway" that opened up a more diverse and expansive world. Phong believes that practical application is essential to mastering a language. He regularly practices speaking English with classmates and native speakers whenever he has the opportunity. In his view, learning a foreign language requires perseverance, and every small improvement deserves recognition. "Don't put too much pressure on yourself or set too many goals. Haste makes waste, and the more stressed you are, the harder it becomes to absorb new knowledge," Phong said. Tran Kim Duyen, head of the foreign languages department at Tran Dai Nghia High School for the Gifted, coached Phong for several years. She described him as a well-rounded student who demonstrated creative thinking, independent learning skills, and a willingness to learn from teachers and peers without becoming arrogant. "Phong is confident, independent and always willing to support those around him. He also helps teachers organize extracurricular activities," she said. Building on his high school experience, Phong hopes to take part in a wide range of activities during his four years at university while striving for strong academic results. He aims to become an English teacher at the high school level. Vietnamese students currently take the same national high school graduation exams, but universities maintain their own admission standards. Institutions are allowed to award additional points, or grant direct admission, to applicants for academic awards, language certificates such as IELTS or SAT, or extracurricular achievements. However, the Ministry of Education and Training recently proposed eliminating university admission bonus points for IELTS certificates and excellent student awards starting next year.
